record.paper_title: Towards Knowledge Exchange: State-of-the-Art and Open Problems
record.original_question: For knowledge-base mapping generation tools, how can complex correspondences be handled when the correspondence says that a function transforms one or more source values into target values, a filter must be imposed on transferred source values, constraints should be added for invented target values, or source values must be aggregated even though knowledge bases use an open-world data model?

evidence.quote: Another type of important correspondence which needs further investigation is complex correspondences which indicate that a function can be used to transform a (set of) source value(s) into a (set of) target value(s), or that a filter should be imposed on source values that are being transferred.

One other interesting example of such correspondences are those that require aggregation over values in the source. Note that aggregating values is not a trivial task specially in KBs since KBs adhere to an open-world data model [18].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider two knowledge bases, a source KB S and a target KB T, each described under an open-world assumption (i.e., absence of a fact is not interpreted as its negation). A schema/instance correspondence is a declarative specification of how data in S relates to data in T. Simple correspondences map a source attribute (or class) directly to a target attribute (or class). A complex correspondence is one that takes any of the following forms:

(a) Functional transformation: there is a function f such that one or more source values v1, …, vk are transformed into one or more target values f(v1, …, vk) (e.g., concatenation, splitting, type conversion, unit conversion).
(b) Filtered transfer: only those source values satisfying a predicate φ are transferred to the target.
(c) Constrained value invention: when a target individual or value must be invented (e.g., a fresh IRI), additional constraints (uniqueness, typing, functional dependencies) must be imposed on the invented term.
(d) Aggregation: a target value is obtained by an aggregate operation (sum, count, average, max, min, group-concatenation, …) over a multiset of source values, taking into account the open-world semantics of S.

Design a general framework for automatic (or semi-automatic) knowledge-base mapping generation tools that:

1. Provides a formal language able to express complex correspondences of types (a)–(d), including a precise semantics under the open-world assumption of both S and T (in particular, give an unambiguous semantics for aggregation in (d) when the source is potentially incomplete).
2. Specifies an algorithm that, given S, T, and a set of complex correspondences in this language, produces an executable mapping (e.g., in a rule language such as R2RML, SPARQL CONSTRUCT, or a Datalog-like formalism) implementing the correspondences.
3. Guarantees correctness properties such as: soundness with respect to the declared correspondences, preservation of target schema constraints introduced in (c), and a well-defined behavior of aggregates in (d) (for instance, by formally distinguishing certain answers from possible answers).

Provide such a framework, or prove that no framework simultaneously achieving (1)–(3) for all four kinds of complex correspondences (a)–(d) exists.
artifact.status_search_result: Handling complex correspondences (functional transformations, filters, constraints on invented IRIs, and aggregation under open-world semantics) in knowledge-base mapping generation is consistently described in recent literature as an open challenge. Surveys on KB matching and mapping generation (e.g., R2RML/RML-based tooling, ontology matching surveys) note that current tools largely handle only simple 1:1 correspondences, with complex and aggregate correspondences identified as an open research direction.

status_evidence.title: Towards Knowledge Exchange: State-of-the-Art and Open Problems (zbMATH)
status_evidence.snippet: Complex correspondences which indicate that a function can be used to transform source values, filters on transferred values, and aggregation over values in the source require further investigation, especially since KBs adhere to an open-world data model.
status_evidence.claim: The problem of supporting complex and aggregate correspondences in KB mapping generation is identified as still open.
